Remark. Electroweak boson masses from vertex \delta q at the CODATA substrate

We apply the local substrate proposition (local substrate q) to electroweak boson mass measurements. This yields a zero-free-parameter formula for the vertex substrate perturbation \delta q.

The vertex \delta q formula

At an interaction vertex (the exceptional divisor \mathcal{S}_p), the gauge-field curvature is non-negligible. The archimedean specialization gives:

  q(p) = 1 + \bigl\lvert\langle L_\varTheta,
  F_A^+\rangle\bigr\rvert(p)
   >  q_0.

The perturbation \delta q = q(p_{\mathrm{vertex}}) - q_0 depends on:

  1. Topological charge at the vertex. \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{top}} = \alpha / (2\pi).
  2. Geometric projection. A single production channel couples to one color tube, yielding a 1/|\chi(\Sigma_4)| = 1/6 factor.

Combining these:

  \boxed{
  \delta q(\text{vertex})
  = 
  (q_0 - 1)
   \cdot 
  \frac{\alpha}{2\pi}
   \cdot 
  \frac{1}{|\chi(\Sigma_4)|}
  }

The mass shift is computed from the sensitivity \partial \ln m / \partial \ln q \approx 9.62:

  \delta m = \frac{\delta q}{q_0}
  \cdot (\partial \ln m / \partial \ln q)
  \cdot m.

CDF–LHC discrepancy

CDF II collided protons with antiprotons. W bosons were produced via valence quark--antiquark annihilation. This compact two-body vertex concentrates gauge-field curvature.

At the LHC, protons lack valence antiquarks. Production requires sea antiquarks (x \sim 0.01--0.05). The effective topological charge is suppressed by x^2:

  \mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{top}}^{\mathrm{sea}}
   \approx 
  \frac{\alpha_W}{2\pi} \cdot x^2
   \sim  10^{-5}.

This drives \delta q below 10^{-6} at the LHC, explaining why ATLAS, CMS, and LHCb measure m_W \approx m_W^{\mathrm{SM}} while CDF observes a 77 MeV excess.

Higgs boson: multi-experiment comparison

The Higgs is produced via gluon--gluon fusion (\alpha = \alpha_s). The vertex \delta q formula predicts \delta q(gg \to H) = 3.4 \times 10^{-4}.

Correlation analysis

We test four patterns against the forward prediction:

1. Collision type (W boson): strongest signal. Match. 2. Decay channel (Higgs): suggestive but noisy. Not statistically significant. 3. Detector B-field: no signal. Consistent with prediction. 4. Collision energy \sqrt{s}: no signal. Consistent with Higgs threshold production.

Experimental tests

  1. CDF versus LHC W mass. The pp^{\sigma}-vs-pp split is the cleanest test.
  2. Higgs \gamma\gamma versus 4\ell across runs. Tests decay-vertex topology dependence.
  3. Half-life measurements in high fields. Shifts would be \approx 0.5\%.
